set.approach: Fly to Kahiltna Base Camp and register with the park mountaineering office in Talkeetna beforehand. From camp, ski or snowshoe south down the Kahiltna Glacier for roughly three to four hours. Once you are past Annie's Ridge the start of the West Ridge comes into view where the ridge drops to meet the glacier. Go around the first rock buttress and head up toward the icefall to begin the climb.
set.descent_text: Hunter has no easy way off, so decide on the way down before leaving the glacier. One option is to retreat the way you came, rappelling what you climbed and downclimbing what you rappelled. The other is to continue to the top of the col that joins the neighbouring Ramen route and descend from there. Both are serious and unfamiliar ground when tired.
hazards: Cornices along the ridge crest
Crevasses on the glacier approach and on the lower ridge
Serac danger below steep ice sections
Tricky route finding between rock, mixed ground and ice
No simple escape from the ridge once committed

review.notes: One page only (MP). Skipped gain: the page lists 8,000 ft without saying what it measures, no second source. Skipped distance and season: none stated on an opened page.

set.approach: After flying to the Kahiltna Glacier, most parties leave the southeast fork near 7,750 feet and head up the northeast fork to the foot of the route, a bergschrund at about 12,200 feet beneath the Japanese Couloir. The climb from the fork to the base is roughly 4,450 feet, and the first stretch is shared with West Rib parties, so a boot track may exist. Travel in the cool hours, when seracs and snow bridges are steadier. A second option is to climb the West Rib cutoff from Genet Basin, join the rib, and descend it to the base.
set.descent_text: After topping out, parties generally go down the West Buttress route, the mountain's standard line, rather than reversing the Cassin itself, and return to the Kahiltna Glacier by that way.
hazards: Open crevasses and weak snow bridges on the northeast fork approach
Avalanche-prone slopes beside the approach in the area nicknamed the Valley of Death
Debris falling into the long Japanese Couloir from the face above
Rockfall in the Chicken Couloir when descending the West Rib to the base
Route finding gets harder and the approach less safe as the season goes on

review.notes: One page (MP). The descent line only restates the existing text plus the fact that West Buttress is the standard route; the MP page gave no detail on the descent. Skipped distance: the page gives no mileage.

set.approach: Fly from Talkeetna onto the Ruth Glacier and land beneath the peak. The base of the West Ridge is about two hours from the landing, over glacier ground that is slow in fresh snow. Above that, a long day in deep snow leads to a high camp near 7,800 feet, from which the lower access couloirs, then a traverse across a steep face to a notch, lead onto the ridge crest.
set.descent_text: Anchors are already in place along much of the route, so the usual way down is a long series of rappels, with downclimbing between them. Shaken Not Stirred, the neighbouring line, has its own anchors and can serve as a bail-out. Expect to be back at the glacier camps late at night after a summit day.
hazards: Large cornices along the ridge, with a corniced summit
Steep loose snow and weak ice that make belays unreliable
Snow mushrooms and a vertical drop on the north side
Serac zone in the icefall between the Ruth Gorge and the Root Canal camp
Deep fresh snow after storms slowing the approach

review.notes: Single trip account for all of it. Skipped gain, distance and season: not stated, and only one May trip is described.

set.approach: Drive to Talkeetna, then fly by ski plane to the west fork of the Tokositna Glacier, which lands directly below the West Face and leaves camp a short walk away. From camp, about an hour of crevasse navigation on the lower glacier leads to a bergschrund crossing and the Access Couloir. Allow a full eight-day trip from Anchorage with weather margin.
set.descent_text: The usual way down is the West Face Couloir, by a series of rappels and some downclimbing. Roughly a dozen v-thread anchors are used. At the bottom, return to the upper basin above base camp and walk a short distance around large crevasses back to camp.
hazards: Crevasses on the glacier and a bergschrund to cross at the base
Sustained 5.9 mixed pitches and an overhanging aid crack on the nose
Rapidly changing weather and snow conditions that dictate the schedule
No easy way off once on the ridge, so the descent must be planned ahead

review.notes: One guide-service page for approach and descent. Final sentence about reversing the Harvard Route is from search results (AAJ trip summaries) and not from an opened page; remove it if reviewers want strict page-only facts. Skipped gain, distance (not stated), season (not stated).

set.approach: Start at the end of the Illecillewaet Campground road, about five kilometres west of Rogers Pass. The Sir Donald trail climbs into the Vaux Glacier basin and on to the Uto-Sir Donald Col, a gain of roughly 4,100 feet taking about two hours for a fit party. A backcountry camping permit is needed for the low bivouac site beside Vaux Creek or the high one at the col. Below the col, take care not to follow a spur trail to campsites by mistake. From the col the arete begins immediately.
set.descent_text: The standard descent follows a bolted rappel line down the northwest ridge, then drops onto the west face for several more stations, after which an easy scramble through scree and ledges leads to the Uto-Sir Donald Col. From the col, walk the trail back to the trailhead. Carry one 50 metre rope, check every anchor, and wait until other parties are clear below you to avoid knocking rock onto them.
hazards: Rockfall onto parties below during the descent, a leading cause of accidents
Mistakes at the rappel stations
Afternoon lightning and fast-changing weather on the exposed ridge
Steep icy snow on the slopes below the col early in the season
No water on the route above the low bivouac

review.notes: Two independent pages for approach and descent; rappel station counts differ (15 stations vs 4+6 rappels) so no count given. Season window is from 'ridge usually free of snow by mid-late July' plus a late August ascent; September not evidenced.

set.approach: From the Kain hut or Applebee camp, allow two to three hours. Climb to the Bugaboo-Snowpatch Col, cross the upper Vowell Glacier westward toward its high point just north of Pigeon Spire, then drop through the Pigeon-Howser Col over big boulders and a steep loose slope to the next glacier. Cross it, avoiding the large crevasses, and swing north to the East Creek bivouac, which sits below the tower. Leaving crampons and an axe at the col saves carrying them for the climb.
set.descent_text: Descend the north face ridge by rappel, then work back toward the east ridge, using newer two-bolt stations with chains and rings. The last rappel crosses a bergschrund onto the Vowell Glacier. A single 70 metre rope covers climbing and descending, and a 60 metre rope has also been enough. Count the rappels from the anchors you find rather than from a topo, as published lengths have been misleading.
hazards: Crevasses on the glacier between the col and the tower
Steep loose slope below the Pigeon-Howser Col
Snow or ice on the rappel ridge making the line hard to hold
Bergschrund at the bottom of the last rappel
Rockfall closures in the area are posted by the park, so check before going

review.notes: One page (MP), whose description is of the Beckey-Chouinard on the west face; the page reports 10 to 11 rappels in comments so no count given. Skipped gain and distance: not stated.

set.descent_text: The descent is by rappel back down the route, using the anchors in place. Some stations may be buried or marginal, so carry extra pitons and cord to strengthen them, and assess each one before weighting it.
hazards: Rockfall below the Woolley Shoulder, where melting ice undermines loose rock
Snow and ice in the upper Japanese gully needing crampons and tools
Buried or unreliable rappel anchors on the descent
Persistent cloud cutting visibility on the face

review.notes: Only one dated conditions report opened. Skipped approach, gain, distance and season: no opened page stated them (the approach includes a river ford and the Woolley Shoulder per search summaries, not opened). 'Mark the way' line is generic advice, drop it if reviewers object.
